text: Pillar names only matter once you've watched them applied to a real system. This lesson runs one concrete architecture through all five pillars, the same way a senior architect runs a real design review — not in the abstract, but against one scenario, end to end.

The scenario: an order-processing API for a mid-size retailer, running as a single AKS or EKS cluster deployed with Terraform, backed by a single-region managed SQL database. Traffic has grown enough that the platform team scheduled a formal review before the next funding cycle — so let's walk it pillar by pillar.

Reliability asks what happens when a dependency fails, not whether the system works today — and here, the cluster and database are both single-region with no documented failover path. Security asks how traffic actually reaches the database and who can touch it: this review turns up a managed identity with subscription-level Contributor access and a database open to the full subnet instead of a private endpoint — an over-permissioned identity and a wider-than-necessary trust boundary.

Cost optimization brings in the FinOps lens from course ten: the cluster is provisioned for Black Friday peak load year-round, at roughly four times average Tuesday demand — though that headroom might be a deliberate reliability tradeoff worth checking before anyone recommends a cut. Operational excellence asks who gets paged and how they roll back, and here there's no on-call routing or rollback runbook at all. Performance efficiency asks whether the resource shape matches the workload — here, a CPU-bound API sits on memory-optimized nodes, mismatched independent of raw capacity.
Here's the real takeaway: the same architecture just produced five distinct, independently true findings, and none of them contradicts another on its own.
But fixing all five at once is where the real architectural work begins, because some of these fixes pull directly against each other — which is exactly the tension the next lesson digs into.
